title: The Filing Association of New York
summary: A newspaper report on the annual meeting of the Filing Association of New York. Unfortunately we all missed it by 104 years.
content:
Via Don, news of the annual meeting of the Filing Association of New York. The after-dinner at Gonfaroni's – closed for 96 years, sadly – sounds like a hoot.

Of course this is charming and quaint, but it makes obvious something that I think about all the time: the fact that, in the past, people used to actively work on the problem of filing. It was a profession; there was a local Association that met regularly.

These filing associations turned into organisations like ARMA, the Association of Records Managers and Administrators. So it's not like we totally forgot how to file stuff. But – at least in my professional experience – it's not something the normal office worker is ever exposed to.

And when filing is something you're forced to do, it tends to be in service of checking a compliance box. Those of us who've had the pleasure of using an enterprise 'document management system' – looking at you, HP TRIM – know that they rarely make a thing easier to find. They just make your mistakes harder to correct.1

Yet it remains the situation that the average office worker is the one creating volumes of stuff; this worker being given little to no training in the still-essential field of filing. No wonder our systems are such a mess.

No wonder nobody can find anything any more.

Footnotes

  1. Every single such system hosting a folder named z_deleted.2 ↩

  2. Addendum: In reading the linked PDF, which I encourage you to at least browse if you've never known the horror of a corporate DMS, I draw your attention to the screenshot on page 42: zDeleted BCS Terms.

    This behaviour is so pervasive it's in the training manual. ↩
